title: Developmental red flags by age (when to refer)
summary: Consolidated age-specific red flags that warrant referral to community paediatrics / child development services. Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) at ANY age is always a red flag requiring urgent assessment.

steps.detail: Regression / loss of any previously attained skill (motor, language, social) - urgent referral. Parental concern about development or hearing/vision should always be taken seriously.
Not smiling responsively (no social smile); not fixing and following; not startling/responding to loud sound.
Persistent primitive reflexes; hand preference (early handedness suggests contralateral weakness); not reaching for objects; persistent squint; very stiff (hypertonia) or very floppy (hypotonia).
Not sitting without support; not babbling; not bearing weight on legs when supported; no response to own name.
No babble, no pointing, no gestures (waving/showing); no single words; not weight-bearing or pulling to stand.
Not walking independently; no clear single words; not pointing to share interest; no functional/pretend play.
No two-word meaningful phrases; persistent toe-walking; cannot follow simple instructions; speech wholly unintelligible to family.
Speech unintelligible to strangers; no interest in other children; frequent falls / abnormal gait.

redFlags: Loss of any developmental skill at any age (regression)
Asymmetry of movement or established hand preference before 18 months
Not walking by 18 months
No words by 18 months
Not sitting by 9 months
No social smile by 8 weeks

title: Autism spectrum disorder: early signs and M-CHAT-R/F screening

sections.heading: Early behavioural signs (social-communication)

Does not respond to own name by 12 months
Does not point to show interest (protodeclarative pointing) or follow a point by 12-18 months

steps.detail: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-up: 20 yes/no parent-report items, validated for 16-30 months. Routine screen at 18 and 24 months.
Total score 0-2 = low risk; 3-7 = medium risk (administer the structured Follow-up interview); 8-20 = high risk (refer directly for diagnostic evaluation and early intervention, bypassing follow-up).
Refer for comprehensive multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment AND to early intervention services without waiting for the diagnosis to be confirmed.

title: Global developmental delay: assessment approach
summary: Global developmental delay (GDD) is significant delay (performance approx 2 SD below the mean, i.e. delay of at least 2 of the developmental domains) in children under 5 years, where reliable IQ testing is not yet possible. It is a clinical description prompting investigation, not a final diagnosis. (Term intellectual disability replaces it from around age 5 once standardised testing is feasible.)

sections.heading: Definition
items: Significant delay (>=2 SD below age expectation) in two or more developmental domains: gross/fine motor, speech/language, cognition, social/personal, activities of daily living
Applies to children under 5 years; reassess as the child matures

steps.detail: Antenatal/perinatal events, prematurity, consanguinity, family history of delay, hearing/vision, regression, seizures, developmental trajectory using a validated tool.
Growth incl. head circumference (micro/macrocephaly), dysmorphic features, neurocutaneous stigmata, tone/power/reflexes, organomegaly, vision and hearing assessment.

Audiology and formal vision assessment in ALL children; then targeted bloods (TFTs, ferritin, U&E, creatine kinase especially in boys with motor delay), and consider chromosomal microarray and Fragile X as first-tier genetic tests.

Neuroimaging (MRI) if microcephaly/macrocephaly, focal signs, regression or seizures; metabolic screen if regression or suggestive features; refer to paediatrician / child development team and early intervention.

redFlags: Developmental regression (loss of skills) - urgent neurology/metabolic referral
Progressive macrocephaly or microcephaly
Focal neurological signs or seizures
Calf hypertrophy / Gowers sign / high CK (consider Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

references.label: AAP / Bright Futures developmental surveillance and screening guidance

title: The four developmental domains: overview for surveillance
summary: Developmental surveillance assesses progress across four domains at every routine contact. Delay isolated to one domain (e.g. language alone) is differentiated from global delay across multiple domains; the pattern guides investigation.

sections.heading: Domains
items: Gross motor - posture, head control, sitting, standing, walking, running, large-muscle coordination
Fine motor / vision - reaching, grasp (palmar to pincer), object manipulation, drawing, eye-hand coordination
Language / speech / hearing - receptive (understanding) and expressive (sounds, words, sentences) communication
Social / emotional / behavioural - interaction, attachment, play, self-care and adaptive skills

steps.detail: For infants born preterm, correct for gestational age (up to about 2 years) before judging milestones.
Milestones follow a predictable sequence; the order and the pattern of delay (isolated vs global) matter as much as exact timing.
Combine routine surveillance with standardised screening at key ages (e.g. 9, 18, 30 months) and act on any parental or clinician concern, missed milestone, or regression.

redFlags: Delay across two or more domains (possible global developmental delay)
Regression in any domain
Discordance between domains warranting targeted assessment (e.g. hearing test for isolated language delay)

title: Weight-for-age (underweight): WHO interpretation
summary: Weight-for-age reflects acute and/or chronic undernutrition combined; it cannot distinguish wasting from stunting and should not be used alone to classify acute malnutrition. Underweight is weight-for-age below -2 SD (z-score) on the WHO Child Growth Standards.

sections.heading: Classification (weight-for-age z-score, WAZ)
items: Normal: WAZ between -2 and +2
Underweight (moderate): WAZ below -2 SD
Severely underweight: WAZ below -3 SD
High weight-for-age (above +2): interpret with weight-for-length/height and BMI-for-age before labelling

steps.detail: Growth monitoring trend over time in children under 5; a flattening or falling trajectory is more informative than a single point.
Does not separate stunting (chronic) from wasting (acute). Use length/height-for-age and weight-for-height (or MUAC) to characterise the type of malnutrition.

redFlags: WAZ below -3 SD (severely underweight) - assess for SAM with weight-for-height/MUAC and oedema
Weight crossing downward through centile spaces over time

title: Length/height-for-age (stunting): WHO interpretation
summary: Length/height-for-age reflects linear growth and indicates CHRONIC undernutrition. Stunting is length/height-for-age below -2 SD on the WHO Child Growth Standards. Measure recumbent length under 2 years (or under 87 cm) and standing height thereafter.

sections.heading: Classification (length/height-for-age z-score, HAZ)
items: Normal: HAZ -2 and above
Stunted (moderate): HAZ below -2 SD
Severely stunted: HAZ below -3 SD

steps.detail: Measure recumbent LENGTH with a length board, two people, child supine, head against fixed end.
Measure standing HEIGHT with a stadiometer, no shoes, heels/buttocks/shoulders against the board, Frankfort plane horizontal.
Length is on average ~0.7 cm greater than standing height; record method used so the correct WHO standard is applied.

redFlags: HAZ below -3 SD (severe stunting)
Progressive crossing of length/height centiles downward (consider chronic disease, endocrine, coeliac)

title: Weight-for-height/length (wasting): WHO interpretation
summary: Weight-for-height (or weight-for-length) reflects ACUTE undernutrition (wasting). Wasting is weight-for-height below -2 SD; severe wasting (weight-for-height below -3 SD) defines severe acute malnutrition (SAM) alongside MUAC <115 mm and/or bilateral pitting oedema.

sections.heading: Classification (weight-for-height z-score, WHZ)
items: Normal: WHZ -2 and above
Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM / moderate wasting): WHZ -3 to below -2 SD
Severe acute malnutrition (SAM / severe wasting): WHZ below -3 SD
Bilateral pitting oedema = SAM regardless of WHZ
Overweight: WHZ above +2; obesity: WHZ above +3 (in under-5s)

steps.detail: Weight-for-height below -3 SD; OR MUAC less than 115 mm; OR bilateral pitting oedema.
Assess appetite (RUTF appetite test) and medical complications; SAM with complications or failed appetite test requires inpatient stabilisation, otherwise outpatient therapeutic care.

redFlags: WHZ below -3 SD = severe acute malnutrition - urgent assessment
Bilateral pitting oedema (kwashiorkor) = always SAM, refer urgently
SAM with poor appetite, oedema, or medical complication = inpatient care

title: MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) screening bands
summary: MUAC is a fast, equipment-light screen for acute malnutrition in children 6-59 months, well suited to community screening. The colour-banded MUAC tape uses red/yellow/green zones at the 115 mm and 125 mm cut-offs.

sections.heading: MUAC bands (children 6-59 months)
items: RED - MUAC less than 115 mm: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) - refer urgently for therapeutic care
YELLOW - MUAC 115 mm to less than 125 mm (>=115 to <125 mm): Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM) - supplementary feeding / close follow-up
GREEN - MUAC 125 mm and above: normal / adequate

steps.detail: Left arm, midpoint between the tip of the shoulder (acromion) and the tip of the elbow (olecranon), arm relaxed and hanging.
Tape snug but not compressing the skin; read to the nearest millimetre. Always also check for bilateral pitting oedema (= SAM irrespective of MUAC).
Validated cut-offs apply to 6-59 months. Different (pregnancy/adolescent/adult) cut-offs apply outside this range.

redFlags: MUAC < 115 mm (red) = SAM - urgent therapeutic feeding referral
Bilateral pitting oedema regardless of MUAC = SAM
MUAC 115-<125 mm (yellow) = MAM - enrol in supplementary feeding and review

title: Z-scores (standard deviation scores): interpretation
summary: A z-score (SD score) is the number of standard deviations a measurement lies above or below the WHO reference median. The -2 SD cut-off is the internationally agreed boundary of normality: by definition only ~2.3% of healthy children fall below -2 SD.

sections.heading: General cut-offs (anthropometric z-scores)
items: Within normal: -2 to +2 SD (captures ~95.4% of healthy children)
Below -2 SD: moderate abnormality (underweight / stunted / wasted depending on index)
Below -3 SD: severe abnormality (severely underweight / stunted / wasted)
Above +2 SD: high (e.g. overweight on weight-for-height or BMI-for-age)
Above +3 SD: very high (e.g. obesity)

steps.detail: Below -2 SD means stunted (height-for-age), wasted (weight-for-height), or underweight (weight-for-age) - the label depends on which index.
-2 SD is agreed for both population surveys and individual flagging, but for an individual always interpret alongside the growth trend and clinical picture.

redFlags: Any index below -3 SD (severe)
Rapidly worsening z-score trajectory over serial measurements

title: BMI-for-age: overweight, obesity and thinness
summary: BMI-for-age is the preferred index for overweight and obesity from 5 years upward (WHO 2007 reference, 5-19 years) and is also used in under-5s (WHO Child Growth Standards). Cut-offs differ between the two age ranges.

sections.heading: Children and adolescents 5-19 years (WHO 2007 reference, z-scores)
items: Overweight: BMI-for-age above +1 SD (approx >=25 kg/m2 equivalent at 19y)
Obesity: BMI-for-age above +2 SD (approx >=30 kg/m2 equivalent at 19y)
Thinness: below -2 SD
Severe thinness: below -3 SD

sections.heading: Children under 5 years (WHO Child Growth Standards, weight-for-height / BMI-for-age z-scores)
items: At risk of overweight: above +1 SD
Overweight: above +2 SD
Obesity: above +3 SD

redFlags: BMI-for-age above +3 SD (obesity in under-5s) - assess for comorbidity and underlying cause
BMI-for-age below -3 SD (severe thinness) - assess for acute malnutrition / chronic disease
Rapid upward BMI crossing centiles in early childhood

references.label: WHO Reference 2007 BMI-for-age 5-19 years
Development of a WHO growth reference for school-aged children (Bull WHO)

title: Head circumference (occipitofrontal circumference): interpretation
summary: Head circumference (occipitofrontal circumference, OFC) tracks brain growth and is plotted on the WHO Child Growth Standards. Serial measurements crossing centiles are more important than a single value. Microcephaly is OFC below -2 SD (<3rd centile); macrocephaly is OFC above +2 SD.

sections.heading: Classification
items: Normal: OFC between -2 and +2 SD
Microcephaly: OFC more than 2 SD below the mean (below approx the 3rd centile)
Severe microcephaly: OFC more than 3 SD below the mean
Macrocephaly: OFC more than 2 SD above the mean for age and sex

steps.detail: Use a non-elastic tape around the maximum occipitofrontal circumference (just above the brows and the most prominent part of the occiput); take the largest of repeated readings.
Plot OFC serially on the WHO chart; a single reading at birth can misclassify - trend over time is essential. Account for prematurity using corrected age.

redFlags: OFC crossing centiles upward with bulging fontanelle / sunsetting eyes (hydrocephalus / raised ICP) - urgent
Progressive microcephaly or arrest of head growth
OFC below -3 SD or above +2 SD warrants assessment and imaging

references.label: WHO Child Growth Standards (head circumference-for-age)
Serial head circumference and classification of congenital microcephaly (BMC Pediatr 2023)

title: Faltering growth (failure to thrive): NICE NG75 approach
summary: Faltering growth describes a slower-than-expected rate of weight (and sometimes length/height) gain in infancy and early childhood. NICE NG75 defines thresholds for concern based on the number of weight centile spaces fallen, weighted by birthweight centile.

sections.heading: NICE NG75 thresholds for concern (sustained fall in weight)
items: A fall across 1 or more weight centile spaces if birthweight was below the 9th centile
A fall across 2 or more weight centile spaces if birthweight was between the 9th and 91st centiles
A fall across 3 or more weight centile spaces if birthweight was above the 91st centile
A current weight below the 2nd centile for age, whatever the birthweight
(A centile space is the distance between two adjacent printed centile lines on the UK-WHO chart)

steps.detail: Plot serial accurate weights (and length/height, head circumference) on the UK-WHO chart; use corrected age if preterm. Beware regression to the mean and measurement error.
Detailed feeding assessment, observe a feed where possible; ask about vomiting, diarrhoea, intake, and psychosocial/family factors.
Full examination; only do investigations guided by clinical findings (NICE advises against routine extensive screening without indication).
Support feeding, increase energy intake, regular weighing at intervals appropriate to age, and refer to paediatric/dietetic services if not responding or if organic cause suspected.

redFlags: Weight below the 2nd centile or sustained fall meeting the NG75 threshold
Faltering growth with dysmorphism, organomegaly, developmental concern, or suspected safeguarding
Acute weight loss or signs of dehydration

references.label: NICE NG75: Faltering growth - recognition and management
NICE QS197: Faltering growth - measurement of growth

title: Catch-up growth: concept and monitoring
summary: Catch-up growth is an accelerated growth velocity (greater than expected for age) that follows a period of growth restriction once the cause is corrected, allowing a child to return towards their genetic growth trajectory. Monitoring confirms recovery and avoids excessive rapid weight gain.

sections.heading: Key points
items: Catch-up growth = growth velocity above the normal range for age, crossing centiles upward toward the pre-illness/genetic channel
Seen after treatment of malnutrition, coeliac disease, hypothyroidism, chronic illness, or after preterm birth
Adequate energy and protein intake is required; in malnutrition recovery, monitor for refeeding syndrome
In faltering growth, expect weight to recover first, then length/height

steps.detail: Plot serial weight and length/height; rising z-scores toward the expected channel indicate catch-up. Use corrected age for preterm infants.
Very rapid weight gain disproportionate to length may signal over-feeding and later metabolic risk; aim for proportionate recovery.

redFlags: Failure to show catch-up despite adequate intake - reassess for organic/endocrine cause
Refeeding syndrome risk during nutritional rehabilitation of severe malnutrition

references.label: Catch-up growth in faltering growth: expert opinion (PMC 2023)
NICE NG75: Faltering growth

title: Growth chart plotting technique
summary: Accurate plotting is the foundation of growth monitoring - errors in age, measurement, or chart choice produce false reassurance or false alarm. Use the correct WHO/UK-WHO chart for sex and age, plot accurately, and interpret the trend.

steps.detail: Sex-specific WHO Child Growth Standards (0-5 years) / WHO 2007 reference (5-19 years); UK-WHO charts where used. Use a preterm/Fenton chart for premature infants and correct for gestation.
Plot weight, length/height and head circumference against the child's exact age (corrected age if born <37 weeks, until ~1-2 years).
Naked or minimal clothing for weight; length board under 2y, stadiometer >=2y; record to standard precision.
Plot a single clear dot (not a cross) at the intersection of age and measurement; join serial points to view the trajectory.
A child normally tracks along a centile; sustained crossing of two or more centile spaces (up or down) warrants review. A single point is rarely diagnostic.

redFlags: Sustained downward crossing of 2+ centile spaces (assess for faltering growth)
Measurement that does not fit the trend - re-measure before acting
Plotting against uncorrected age in a preterm infant (false faltering)

references.label: WHO Child Growth Standards - training and chart use
NICE QS197: Faltering growth - measurement of growth

title: Mid-parental (target) height calculation
summary: Mid-parental height estimates a child's genetic height potential from parental heights, providing a target range against which the child's projected adult height is compared. A child tracking well below their target range may warrant endocrine assessment.

sections.heading: Calculation
items: Mid-parental height = average of mother's and father's heights
Boys: add 6.5 cm to the parental average (i.e. (father + mother + 13 cm) / 2)
Girls: subtract 6.5 cm from the parental average (i.e. (father + mother - 13 cm) / 2)
Target height range: approximately the calculated value plus or minus 8.5 cm (captures ~94% of healthy children)

steps.detail: Plot the target height (and range) on the chart at adult age; the child's current centile should be broadly consistent with the target range.
Predicted adult height markedly below the target range, or short stature with falling height velocity, suggests a pathological cause - refer for assessment (e.g. endocrine, coeliac, chronic disease).

redFlags: Height velocity falling / crossing centiles downward with predicted height below target range
Marked discrepancy between child's height centile and mid-parental target

references.label: Accurate prediction of children's target height from mid-parental height (PMC 2024)

title: Percentiles vs z-scores: interpretation in growth monitoring
summary: Growth charts display centile (percentile) lines; clinical/nutritional surveys often use z-scores. Both describe a child's position relative to the reference; understanding their relationship prevents misinterpretation, particularly at the extremes.

sections.heading: Key relationships
items: 50th centile = median = z-score 0
2nd-3rd centile is approximately -2 SD (the conventional lower limit of normal)
97th-98th centile is approximately +2 SD (upper limit of normal)
0.4th centile is approximately -2.67 SD; 99.6th centile approximately +2.67 SD (outermost UK-WHO lines)
Below the 2nd centile or below -2 SD flags the child for review

steps.detail: Centile lines are intuitive for plotting individual children and tracking trajectory.
Z-scores quantify how far beyond -2 SD a child lies (e.g. -3 vs -4 SD), which centiles cannot show once off the chart; they are standard for population nutrition data and SAM classification.

redFlags: Measurement below the 0.4th centile / below -2.67 SD (off the printed chart) - assess and quantify with z-score
Crossing centile lines rather than tracking

references.label: WHO Child Growth Standards (centiles and z-scores)
What is normal growth? Principles and pitfalls (Ann Nutr Metab, Karger)

title: Acute malnutrition classification (IMAM): SAM, MAM and oedema
summary: The Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) approach (Kenya MOH / WHO) classifies children 6-59 months by degree of wasting and by oedema to direct them into the correct care stream. Bilateral pitting oedema always denotes SAM.

sections.heading: Classification (children 6-59 months)
items: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM): MUAC < 115 mm, OR weight-for-height below -3 SD, OR bilateral pitting oedema (any grade)
Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM): MUAC 115 to <125 mm, OR weight-for-height -3 to below -2 SD, AND no oedema
No acute malnutrition: MUAC >=125 mm AND weight-for-height -2 SD or above AND no oedema

steps.detail: Apply gentle thumb pressure to the top of both feet for 3 seconds; a persisting pit (indentation) confirms oedema. Bilateral oedema = SAM and requires referral/treatment.

SAM + medical complication or failed appetite test or oedema grade +++ -> inpatient (stabilisation) care; uncomplicated SAM with appetite -> outpatient therapeutic programme with RUTF; MAM -> supplementary feeding programme.

redFlags: Bilateral pitting oedema = SAM regardless of MUAC/weight-for-height - refer
MUAC < 115 mm or weight-for-height < -3 SD = SAM
SAM with poor appetite, danger signs, or medical complication = urgent inpatient stabilisation

references.label: Kenya National Guideline for Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM)
WHO Child Growth Standards and identification of SAM

title: Newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE)
summary: The NIPE is a head-to-toe screening examination offered within 72 hours of birth and repeated at 6-8 weeks. It specifically screens four areas - eyes, heart, hips, and (in boys) testes - to detect congenital abnormalities early.

steps.detail: Inspect for symmetry/size; elicit the red reflex bilaterally with an ophthalmoscope (absent/white reflex may indicate congenital cataract or retinoblastoma) - screens for congenital eye abnormalities.

Inspect colour/work of breathing; auscultate heart sounds and murmurs; palpate femoral pulses (weak/absent suggests coarctation); check for cyanosis - screens for critical congenital heart disease (pre/post-ductal saturations where protocol includes pulse oximetry).
Perform Barlow (provocation to dislocate) and Ortolani (reduction) manoeuvres; assess for leg-length discrepancy and asymmetric skin creases - screens for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
Palpate both testes in the scrotum - screens for undescended testis (cryptorchidism).

sections.heading: General examination also includes
items: Tone, posture and movement; fontanelles and sutures; palate (cleft); spine (for sacral dimple/spina bifida occulta signs); abdomen and genitalia; femoral pulses; skin and birthmarks; weight and head circumference

redFlags: Absent or white (leucocoria) red reflex - urgent ophthalmology (cataract/retinoblastoma)
Absent/weak femoral pulses or murmur with cyanosis - urgent cardiology (coarctation/CHD)
Positive Barlow/Ortolani or hip click with asymmetry - hip ultrasound for DDH
Bilateral undescended/impalpable testes - urgent review (consider DSD)

references.label: NHS NIPE screening programme handbook (GOV.UK)

title: Newborn hearing screening (UNHS)
summary: Universal newborn hearing screening detects permanent congenital hearing loss early to enable timely intervention. Physiological screening is done before discharge / by 1 month, using otoacoustic emissions (OAE) and/or automated auditory brainstem response (AABR).

sections.heading: Methods
items: Otoacoustic emissions (OAE): measures cochlear (outer hair cell) response; quick, screens the outer/middle/inner ear up to the cochlea

Automated auditory brainstem response (AABR): measures the response along the auditory nerve and brainstem; detects auditory neuropathy that OAE may miss; used for NICU babies and as a second-stage screen

steps.detail: All newborns screened with a physiological measure before hospital discharge, no later than 1 month of age.
Infants who do not pass screening receive full audiological diagnostic assessment no later than 3 months of age.
Infants confirmed deaf or hard of hearing are enrolled in early intervention as soon as possible, no later than 6 months of age.

redFlags: No clear response (refer result) on screening - timely diagnostic audiology, do not wait
Risk factors (NICU >5 days, hyperbilirubinaemia requiring exchange, congenital infection, family history) - ongoing surveillance even if screen passed
Parental concern about hearing at any age - refer for audiology

references.label: AAP Hearing Assessment in Infants, Children, and Adolescents (Pediatrics 2023)
CDC Newborn Hearing Screening

title: Vision screening in children
summary: Vision screening across childhood aims to detect treatable causes of visual impairment and amblyopia early, when intervention is most effective. It begins with the newborn red reflex and progresses to age-appropriate acuity testing.

steps.detail: Red reflex at NIPE and at 6-8 week check (white reflex/leucocoria, absent or asymmetric red reflex requires urgent ophthalmology for cataract/retinoblastoma); observe fixing and following and assess for squint.
Inspection for strabismus (cover test, corneal light reflex), assessment of fixation and visual behaviour; refer manifest squint.
Orthoptist-led visual acuity screening to detect amblyopia and refractive error before school entry - the window for amblyopia treatment is in early childhood.
Acuity testing with age-appropriate charts; refer reduced acuity, squint, or symptoms for ophthalmology/optometry.

redFlags: Absent or white red reflex (leucocoria) - urgent same-day ophthalmology (retinoblastoma/cataract)
Manifest squint beyond ~3 months of age - refer (risk of amblyopia)
Reduced or asymmetric visual acuity - refer for assessment before the amblyopia treatment window closes

references.label: NHS NIPE screening programme handbook (eyes / red reflex)
AAP / Bright Futures vision screening recommendations

title: Developmental surveillance and screening schedule
summary: Developmental surveillance (ongoing observation and parental concern at every visit) is combined with standardised developmental screening at defined ages, and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months, per AAP/Bright Futures. Surveillance plus screening detects more delay than either alone.

steps.detail: Developmental surveillance: elicit and act on parental concerns, take a developmental history, observe the child, and review milestones.
Administer a validated general developmental screening tool (e.g. ASQ) at these visits.
Administer an autism-specific screening tool (M-CHAT-R/F).
If surveillance, screening, or a parent raises concern, perform screening promptly and refer for diagnostic evaluation and early intervention - do not adopt watchful waiting alone.

redFlags: Failed developmental or autism screen - refer for evaluation AND early intervention concurrently
Loss of skills at any age
Persistent parental concern despite a passed screen - re-screen / refer

references.label: CDC Developmental Milestones / Learn the Signs. Act Early.
AAP Bright Futures periodicity and surveillance guidance

title: Denver II developmental screening test: overview
summary: The Denver Developmental Screening Test (Denver II) is a screening tool to identify possible developmental problems in children from birth to 6 years across four domains. It screens (flags children needing further assessment); it is not a diagnostic or IQ test.

sections.heading: Structure
items: Age range: birth to 6 years
125 items across four domains: personal-social (25), fine motor-adaptive (29), language (39), gross motor (32)
Items are plotted against an age line; each item shows the age range over which 25%, 50%, 75% and 90% of children pass
Takes approximately 20 minutes; results classified as normal, suspect, or untestable

steps.detail: Interaction with people and self-care (e.g. waving bye-bye, dressing, feeding self).
Eye-hand coordination, manipulation of small objects, problem solving (e.g. stacking blocks, drawing).
Hearing, understanding and use of language - receptive and expressive.
Sitting, walking, jumping and large-muscle coordination.

redFlags: A suspect result (delays/cautions) - rescreen and/or refer for formal developmental assessment
Screening is not diagnostic - a failed screen always requires confirmatory evaluation

references.label: Denver Developmental Screening Tests (overview)
Denver Developmental Screening Test (ScienceDirect topic overview)

title: Growth monitoring schedule
summary: Routine growth monitoring plots weight, length/height and head circumference over time to detect faltering growth, overweight and microcephaly/macrocephaly early. Frequency is highest in infancy and reduces as the child grows; trend matters more than a single measurement.

sections.heading: Indicative frequency (well children)
items: At birth and within the first week (assess weight loss / regain)
Routinely at immunisation and well-child contacts through infancy (commonly monthly in the first 6 months, then at intervals through the first 1-2 years)
Head circumference plotted regularly through infancy (e.g. birth, 6-8 weeks, and at routine reviews)
Less frequent measurement in healthy older children; increase frequency if growth concern arises

steps.detail: Per NICE, do not weigh too often - measurement noise can mimic faltering; space weights appropriately to age (a single low reading is not faltering).
Use the correct WHO/UK-WHO chart and corrected age for preterm infants; review trajectory and act on sustained centile crossing.

redFlags: Excessive newborn weight loss (>10% birthweight) or failure to regain birthweight by 2-3 weeks
Sustained centile crossing (faltering growth or rapid excessive gain)
Head circumference crossing centiles

references.label: NICE QS197: Faltering growth - measurement of growth
WHO Child Growth Standards

title: MUAC community screening for acute malnutrition
summary: MUAC measurement with a colour-banded tape is the cornerstone of community-level screening for acute malnutrition in children 6-59 months, and can be performed by community health workers (and family members in Family-MUAC approaches) to refer children before they decompensate.

steps.detail: Children 6-59 months in the community; screen at health contacts, outreach and household visits.
Left mid-upper arm, midpoint acromion-olecranon; read the colour band. Always also check both feet for bilateral pitting oedema.

RED (<115 mm) or any bilateral oedema: refer urgently for SAM treatment. YELLOW (115-<125 mm): refer to supplementary feeding for MAM. GREEN (>=125 mm): healthy nutrition advice and routine follow-up.

sections.heading: Notes
items: MUAC is simple, low-cost, reproducible and strongly predictive of mortality risk, making it ideal for community screening
Family-MUAC programmes train caregivers to measure and seek care early
Confirm and stream referred children at the facility using full anthropometry and clinical assessment

redFlags: MUAC < 115 mm (red) or bilateral pitting oedema - urgent referral for SAM care
Any child with danger signs (lethargy, not feeding, convulsions, dehydration) - emergency referral irrespective of MUAC

references.label: WHO Child Growth Standards and identification of SAM (MUAC cut-offs)
Accuracy of MUAC to detect wasting in children 6-59 months (Glob Health Sci Pract)

title: Immunisation-linked opportunistic screening
summary: Routine immunisation visits are key opportunities to deliver opportunistic child-health screening - growth monitoring, developmental surveillance, nutrition (MUAC), and feeding/safeguarding review - because attendance is high in early childhood. Integrating these is endorsed by WHO and Kenya MOH MCH services.

sections.heading: What to combine at immunisation contacts
items: Plot weight (and length/head circumference at appropriate visits) on the growth chart
Developmental surveillance: review milestones and elicit parental concerns
Nutrition screen: MUAC and check for oedema in the 6-59 month age group; assess feeding
Check the immunisation record is up to date and catch up missed doses
Vitamin A and deworming where part of the national programme; review for danger signs

steps.detail: Infants and toddlers attend repeatedly for vaccines; bundling screening maximises detection of growth faltering and developmental delay with no extra visit.
Refer flagged children (faltering growth, MUAC red/yellow, missed milestones, missed vaccines) into the appropriate care pathway.

redFlags: Missed milestones or regression identified opportunistically - refer
MUAC red/yellow or faltering weight at a vaccine visit - nutrition referral
Defaulting from the immunisation schedule - active catch-up and follow-up

references.label: WHO recommendations on routine immunisation and integrated MCH services
WHO Child Growth Standards

title: Primitive reflexes and timing of integration
summary: Primitive reflexes are automatic, brainstem-mediated movements present in the newborn that are normally suppressed (integrated) as the cortex matures. Their presence at birth is reassuring; persistence beyond the expected age, asymmetry, or absence when expected are red flags for a neurological problem (e.g. cerebral palsy).

sections.heading: Common primitive reflexes and expected integration

steps.detail: Sudden head extension causes symmetrical arm abduction/extension then adduction. Present from birth; normally disappears by 3-4 months (may persist to ~6 months). Asymmetry suggests brachial plexus injury or fracture; persistence beyond 6 months is abnormal.

Stroking the cheek makes the infant turn the head and open the mouth toward the stimulus. Present from birth (appears ~28 weeks gestation); fades around 4 months as feeding comes under voluntary control.
Pressure on the palm produces finger flexion/grasp. Present from birth; integrates around 5-6 months (releases ~3-6 months as voluntary grasp develops).

Turning the head to one side extends the limbs on that side and flexes the contralateral limbs. Appears in the early weeks; normally integrates by about 6-7 months, allowing symmetrical movement and rolling/crawling.
Sucking present from birth, integrates over the first months; the stepping (walking) reflex is present at birth and typically disappears around 2 months.

redFlags: Persistence of primitive reflexes beyond the expected age (e.g. Moro beyond 6 months, ATNR beyond 6-7 months) - possible cerebral palsy / neurological abnormality
Asymmetry of a reflex (e.g. asymmetric Moro suggesting brachial plexus injury, clavicle fracture, or hemiplegia)
Absence of a reflex when it should be present (suggests CNS depression or neuromuscular disorder)

references.label: Primitive Reflexes - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)

title: Speech-sound development and intelligibility by age
summary: Speech intelligibility (how much of a child's speech an unfamiliar listener understands) increases predictably with age and is a practical screen for speech delay. Familiar listeners understand more than strangers. Some later-developing sounds normally remain immature until school age.

sections.heading: Intelligibility to an unfamiliar listener (rule of quarters)
items: By age 2 years: about 50% intelligible
By age 3 years: about 75% intelligible
By age 4 years: about 90-100% intelligible (speech largely understandable to strangers)

sections.heading: Order of consonant acquisition
items: Early sounds (mastered ~by 2-3 years): /p/, /b/, /m/, /n/, /w/, /h/
Most English consonants are acquired by 4-5 years
Later-developing sounds may not be fully mastered until ~7-8 years: /r/, /l/, /s/, /z/, 'th', and consonant clusters
Phonological simplification processes (e.g. cluster reduction: 'plane' to 'pane') normally resolve between 3 and 5 years

redFlags: Speech largely unintelligible to family by 2 years or to strangers by 3 years - refer for speech-language and hearing assessment
Loss of previously acquired speech (regression) at any age
No words by 18 months / no two-word phrases by 2 years (also assess hearing)

references.label: Speech Sound Development Chart (Expressable, citing intelligibility norms)
Speech development between 30 and 119 months: intelligibility growth curves (J Speech Lang Hear Res 2021)

title: Toilet-training readiness
summary: The AAP recommends a child-oriented approach: begin only when the child shows readiness signs rather than at a fixed age. Most children show readiness signs around 18 months, training is commonly started around 24 months, and daytime dryness is usually achieved by 30-36 months. Starting before 24 months is generally not recommended.

sections.heading: Readiness signs (physical, cognitive, emotional)
items: Physical: can walk steadily, sit and squat, pull clothing up/down, and stays dry for longer periods (e.g. through a nap) indicating sphincter control
Cognitive: understands and follows simple instructions; has words for urine/stool and toileting
Emotional/behavioural: shows awareness of a full bladder/bowel, dislikes a soiled nappy and asks to be changed, imitates toileting, and shows a desire to use the potty/toilet

sections.heading: Approach
items: Use a child-oriented (readiness-based) method; do not force training before the child is developmentally, emotionally and behaviourally ready
Most children are ready around 18-24 months; some later - delay is normal
Use praise/positive reinforcement; expect setbacks and night-time dryness to come later than daytime

redFlags: No daytime continence by ~4 years, or secondary loss of acquired continence - assess (constipation, UTI, neurological/behavioural cause)
Painful, stool-withholding or distressing patterns - pause training and address constipation

references.label: AAP Toilet Training Guidelines (Pediatrics)
Toilet Training: Common Questions and Answers (AAFP 2019)

title: School readiness assessment
summary: School readiness is the child's developmental preparedness (across physical, social-emotional, language/communication, cognitive and approaches-to-learning domains) to engage successfully with formal schooling. It is multi-domain and not just academic; the CDC 5-year milestones approximate the skills expected at school entry.

sections.heading: Domains of readiness
items: Social-emotional: follows rules and takes turns, separates from caregiver, manages feelings, plays cooperatively
Language and communication: tells a simple story, holds a back-and-forth conversation, understands and follows instructions
Cognitive / pre-academic: counts to ~10, recognises some letters/numbers, attends to a non-screen task for 5-10 minutes
Physical / self-care: hops on one foot, holds a pencil with a tripod grasp, dresses and toilets independently, washes hands

sections.heading: Practical points
items: Assess all domains - a child strong academically may lag in social-emotional readiness (and vice versa)
Address vision and hearing before school entry (untreated deficits impair learning)
Refer children with persistent delay for developmental assessment and early intervention before school start

redFlags: Cannot give first and last name or follow simple multi-step instructions at 5 years
Persistent difficulty separating, regulating behaviour, or interacting with peers
Unrecognised vision or hearing impairment
Any loss of skills

references.label: CDC Developmental Milestones (5 years) - Learn the Signs. Act Early.

title: Tanner stages (sexual maturity rating): adolescent development overview
summary: Tanner staging (Sexual Maturity Rating, SMR) classifies pubertal development from stage 1 (prepubertal) to stage 5 (adult). In girls it grades breast and pubic hair development; in boys it grades genital and pubic hair development. It is used to assess timing of puberty and detect precocious or delayed puberty.

sections.heading: Girls (breast B1-B5; pubic hair P1-P5)
items: Stage 1: prepubertal - no breast tissue, no pubic hair
Stage 2: breast bud (thelarche, the first sign of puberty in girls, typically ~8-13 years); sparse downy pubic hair
Stage 3: further enlargement of breast and areola without separation of contours; coarser, darker, curlier hair spreading over the pubis
Stage 4: areola and papilla form a secondary mound projecting above the breast; adult-type hair not yet spread to the thighs
Stage 5: mature breast (areola recesses to general breast contour); adult pubic hair extending to the medial thighs. Menarche usually occurs in stage 3-4.

sections.heading: Boys (genital G1-G5; pubic hair P1-P5)
items: Stage 1: prepubertal - testes, scrotum and penis childhood size; no pubic hair
Stage 2: testicular and scrotal enlargement (testicular volume >=4 mL is the first sign of puberty in boys, typically ~9-14 years); scrotal skin reddens/thins; sparse hair at base of penis
Stage 3: penis lengthens; testes/scrotum grow further; hair darker, coarser, curlier
Stage 4: penis grows in length and breadth; glans develops; scrotum darkens; adult-type hair not yet on thighs
Stage 5: adult genitalia; adult pubic hair spreading to medial thighs

redFlags: Onset of puberty before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys (precocious puberty) - refer endocrinology
No breast development by 13 in girls or no testicular enlargement by 14 in boys (delayed puberty) - investigate
Discordance (e.g. pubic hair without gonadal enlargement) suggesting an adrenal/exogenous androgen source

references.label: Tanner Stages - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)

title: Weight velocity (rate of weight gain) in infancy
summary: Weight velocity is the rate of weight gain over time and is more sensitive to acute nutritional problems than a single weight. Expected gain is highest in early infancy and slows steadily. High day-to-day variability is normal, so judge velocity over an appropriate interval, not single weighings.

sections.heading: Approximate expected weight gain (term infants)
items: Newborns typically lose up to ~7-10% of birthweight in the first days and regain birthweight by 10-14 days
0-3 months: about 25-30 g/day on average (roughly 1 oz/day)
3-6 months: about 15-20 g/day (roughly 0.5-0.7 oz/day)
6-12 months: gain slows further; birthweight roughly doubles by ~4-5 months and trebles by ~12 months
Day-to-day variability is high and normal - assess velocity over weeks, not single weighings

steps.detail: Do not weigh too frequently; short-interval weights are dominated by measurement noise and normal variation and can mimic faltering.
Sustained low velocity with downward centile crossing suggests faltering growth (assess per NICE NG75); excessive rapid gain (>45 g/day in the first 2 months) may signal overfeeding.

redFlags: Failure to regain birthweight by 2-3 weeks or weight loss >10% of birthweight
Sustained low weight velocity with downward centile crossing (faltering growth)
Excessive rapid weight gain disproportionate to length

references.label: WHO Child Growth Standards (weight velocity)
NICE NG75: Faltering growth

title: Height (length) velocity and growth-velocity assessment
summary: Height (length) velocity - the rate of linear growth per year - is the most sensitive index of a growth disorder, often abnormal before height centile crossing is obvious. A low or falling height velocity warrants endocrine and systemic evaluation even if absolute height is still within the normal range.

sections.heading: Approximate normal linear growth
items: Infancy (0-12 months): ~25 cm in the first year (rapid, nutrition-dependent phase)
Second year: ~12 cm/year
Mid-childhood (after ~3 years to puberty): steady, roughly 5-7 cm/year (a velocity below ~4-5 cm/year in this phase is a concern)
Puberty: growth spurt - peak height velocity (commonly ~8-12 cm/year), earlier in girls than boys

steps.detail: Calculate velocity from two accurate height/length measurements at least 6-12 months apart (shorter intervals are unreliable due to measurement error and seasonal variation).

A subnormal or declining height velocity (downward centile crossing) suggests a pathological cause - assess for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, coeliac disease, chronic systemic disease, and obtain a bone age.

redFlags: Height velocity persistently below the normal range for age (e.g. <4-5 cm/year in mid-childhood) or crossing centiles downward
Short stature with low growth velocity (more concerning than short stature with normal velocity)
Falling height velocity with weight gain (suggests endocrine cause e.g. hypothyroidism, Cushing)

references.label: Evaluation of Short and Tall Stature in Children (AAFP 2015)
WHO Child Growth Standards

title: Bone age (skeletal maturity): concept and use
summary: Bone age is an estimate of skeletal maturity from a radiograph of the left hand and wrist, classically compared with the Greulich and Pyle atlas. Comparing bone age with chronological age helps differentiate causes of abnormal growth and predict remaining growth potential.

sections.heading: Method
items: A single radiograph of the LEFT hand and wrist is compared with standard atlas images (Greulich & Pyle, 1959) to assign a skeletal age
Carpal bones, metacarpals and phalangeal epiphyses are assessed for ossification and fusion
Low radiation dose; interrater variability exists (automated methods e.g. BoneXpert reduce this)

steps.step: Delayed bone age (bone age < chronological age)
steps.detail: Seen in constitutional delay of growth and puberty, hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, chronic illness and malnutrition - implies greater remaining growth potential.

steps.step: Advanced bone age (bone age > chronological age)
steps.detail: Seen in precocious puberty, obesity, hyperthyroidism, and excess sex steroids/androgens - implies reduced remaining growth and earlier epiphyseal fusion.

steps.step: Normal bone age in short stature
steps.detail: Bone age equal to chronological age in a short child suggests familial (genetic) short stature rather than a delay that will catch up.

redFlags: Markedly advanced bone age with early secondary sexual characteristics (precocious puberty) - refer endocrinology
Significantly delayed bone age with poor growth velocity - investigate (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, coeliac, chronic disease)

title: Short stature: evaluation approach
summary: Short stature is usually defined as height below the 2nd-3rd centile (about -2 SD) or significantly below the mid-parental target range. Growth velocity is the key discriminator: short stature with a normal velocity is usually a normal variant, while a low/falling velocity points to a pathological cause needing investigation.

sections.heading: Common normal variants
items: Familial (genetic) short stature: short parents, height appropriate for mid-parental target, normal velocity, normal (non-delayed) bone age
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty: delayed bone age and delayed puberty, often a family history, with eventual normal adult height

steps.detail: Accurate height/length, weight, and calculate growth velocity and mid-parental (target) height; plot serially on the correct chart.
Birth/perinatal history, chronic symptoms, nutrition, drugs (e.g. steroids), dysmorphism, pubertal stage, disproportion (limb vs trunk suggests skeletal dysplasia).
Bone age (left hand/wrist) plus screening bloods: TFTs, coeliac serology, FBC, U&E/creatinine, LFTs, bone profile, and consider IGF-1; karyotype in girls to exclude Turner syndrome.
Refer to paediatric endocrinology if growth velocity is low/falling, height is disproportionately below target, or screening tests are abnormal; growth hormone testing is specialist-led.

redFlags: Short stature with a low or declining growth velocity (pathological until proven otherwise)
Height well below the mid-parental target range
Disproportion, dysmorphism, or abnormal screening bloods
All short girls: consider and exclude Turner syndrome (karyotype)

title: Tall stature: evaluation approach
summary: Tall stature is height above the ~97th-98th centile (about +2 SD) or markedly above the mid-parental target. The great majority is familial (constitutional) and benign; pathology is uncommon (~1.5% of referrals) but important syndromes (notably Marfan) must not be missed.

sections.heading: Causes
items: Familial (constitutional) tall stature: tall parents, height parallels a high centile, normal pace of puberty, normal bone age, no dysmorphism - usually no investigation needed

Pathological (uncommon): Marfan syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), homocystinuria, growth-hormone excess, precocious puberty (early tall but reduced final height), obesity (accelerates growth/bone age)

steps.detail: Plot serial heights, calculate mid-parental target and predicted adult height, and determine bone age.
Assess body proportions, arm span, joint laxity, lens/cardiac signs (Marfan), and pubertal staging - exclude Marfan and Klinefelter where features suggest them.
Investigate only if pathology suspected (e.g. karyotype for Klinefelter, echocardiography/ophthalmology and genetics for Marfan, IGF-1 for GH excess).

redFlags: Marfanoid features (tall, arm span > height, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, aortic root dilatation) - urgent assessment, do not miss Marfan
Tall boy with small firm testes / learning difficulties (consider Klinefelter)
Accelerating growth with advanced bone age and early puberty

title: Childhood overweight and obesity classification
summary: In children and teens (2-19 years) overweight and obesity are defined by sex-specific BMI-for-age percentiles, not adult absolute BMI thresholds, because children are still growing. The CDC growth references are used in the US; WHO references are used elsewhere (cut-offs differ).

sections.heading: CDC BMI-for-age categories (2-19 years)
items: Underweight: below the 5th percentile
Healthy weight: 5th to below the 85th percentile
Overweight: 85th to below the 95th percentile
Obesity: at or above the 95th percentile
Severe obesity: BMI >= 120% of the 95th percentile (or >= 35 kg/m2)

sections.heading: Notes
items: WHO 2007 reference (5-19 years) uses z-scores: overweight >+1 SD, obesity >+2 SD; under-5s use weight-for-height/BMI-for-age (overweight >+2 SD, obesity >+3 SD)
Use the correct reference for the population and state which one was used
Assess for comorbidity (blood pressure, lipids, glucose, NAFLD) and underlying/syndromic causes, especially with short stature or developmental concern

redFlags: Severe obesity (>=120% of the 95th percentile) - assess cardiometabolic comorbidity
Obesity WITH short stature or developmental delay - consider endocrine (hypothyroidism, Cushing) or genetic/syndromic cause
Rapid upward BMI centile crossing

title: Waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio in children
summary: Waist circumference measures central (abdominal) adiposity, which is more strongly linked to cardiometabolic risk than BMI alone. Because waist circumference changes with growth and puberty, the waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) is a convenient age-independent screen in children.

sections.heading: Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR)
items: WHtR = waist circumference / height (same units)
A widely used screening cut-off is 0.5 - 'keep your waist to less than half your height' (meta-analysis optimal pooled cut-off ~0.49)
WHtR >= 0.5 flags central obesity and increased cardiometabolic risk - assess BMI, blood pressure and metabolic profile
WHtR varies little with age and only slightly by sex, making a single cut-off practical across childhood

steps.detail: Measure waist circumference with a non-stretch tape at a standardised landmark (commonly the midpoint between the lowest rib and the iliac crest, or at the umbilicus per protocol) at the end of normal expiration; keep the tape horizontal and snug.
Use WHtR alongside BMI-for-age; an elevated ratio prompts assessment for comorbidity and lifestyle intervention. Ethnic-specific thresholds may apply.

redFlags: WHtR >= 0.5 (central obesity) - assess blood pressure, lipids, glucose and liver
Central obesity with acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance) or hypertension

references.label: Optimal WHtR cut-off to predict central obesity in children and adolescents: systematic review and meta-analysis (Front Nutr 2022)

title: MUAC in pregnancy: maternal undernutrition screening
summary: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is the preferred anthropometric screen for acute undernutrition in pregnancy because BMI is unreliable in pregnancy and MUAC changes little across gestation, requires no gestational dating, and is simple for community settings. Low MUAC predicts low birthweight.

sections.heading: Cut-offs (pregnant and lactating women)
items: No single global consensus cut-off; programmes commonly use MUAC < 23 cm (a conservative threshold capturing most at risk of low birthweight in African/Asian contexts)
Lower thresholds (< 21 cm or < 22 cm) are used in some humanitarian programmes to define acute maternal malnutrition for therapeutic feeding
MUAC does not change significantly during pregnancy and does not need gestational age - an advantage over weight/BMI

steps.detail: Left mid-upper arm, midpoint between acromion and olecranon, arm relaxed; tape snug, read to the nearest millimetre - same technique as paediatric MUAC.
Enrol women below the programme cut-off in supplementary/therapeutic feeding and antenatal nutrition support; counsel on diet and monitor gestational weight gain and fetal growth.

redFlags: MUAC below the programme cut-off (commonly < 23 cm, or < 21 cm for therapeutic feeding) - enrol in maternal nutrition support; risk of low birthweight
Poor gestational weight gain or signs of fetal growth restriction

title: Newborn bloodspot (heel-prick / Guthrie) screening
summary: The newborn bloodspot test (historically the Guthrie test) is taken by heel-prick, typically around day 5 of life, to detect rare but serious treatable conditions before symptoms appear. The UK programme screens for nine conditions; panels differ by country (US RUSP is broader).

sections.heading: UK panel (nine conditions)
items: Phenylketonuria (PKU)
Congenital hypothyroidism (CHT)
Sickle cell disease (SCD)
Cystic fibrosis (CF)
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD)
Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD)
Isovaleric acidaemia (IVA)
Glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1)
Homocystinuria (HCU)

steps.detail: Take the sample around day 5 (ideally day 5-8); for some analytes (e.g. TSH) sampling before 24-48h can give false results. Offer up to 1 year of age if missed.
Warm clean foot, heel-prick the lateral/medial plantar heel, fill all circles of the card with well-formed blood spots; allow to dry; record on the correct card.
A screen-positive result requires prompt confirmatory testing and referral; screening identifies risk, it is not diagnostic.

redFlags: A positive newborn bloodspot screen needs urgent confirmatory testing and specialist referral - do not delay
Sample taken too early (before 24-48h) or insufficient spot - repeat
Sick or symptomatic neonate - do not rely on screening; investigate and treat on clinical grounds

title: Congenital hypothyroidism: newborn screening
summary: Congenital hypothyroidism is one of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability. Newborn bloodspot screening (primary TSH, or T4 with backup TSH) detects it before symptoms, and early levothyroxine treatment prevents the severe neurodevelopmental harm of late diagnosis.

sections.heading: Screening
items: Detected on the newborn bloodspot, usually by a raised TSH (primary TSH strategy with backup T4), aiming to diagnose within the first 2-3 weeks of life
Heel-prick taken after 24-48 hours to avoid false positives from the physiological neonatal TSH surge
A screen-positive result triggers urgent confirmatory venous TSH/free T4 and referral

steps.detail: Begin levothyroxine as soon as confirmatory bloods are taken, without waiting for results; typical starting dose is about 10-15 micrograms/kg/day.
Starting treatment late (e.g. after 30 days), at low dose, or in severe cases is associated with poorer neurocognitive outcome; early adequate treatment normalises development.

redFlags: Screen-positive (raised TSH) - urgent confirmatory bloods and same-week specialist referral, start levothyroxine without delay
Clinical features (prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, hypotonia, large fontanelle, constipation) - test regardless of screen
Delayed treatment risks irreversible intellectual disability

title: SCID and cystic fibrosis newborn screening
summary: Two bloodspot screens with very different first-tier markers: SCID is screened by the T-cell receptor excision circle (TREC) assay (a marker of T-cell production), and cystic fibrosis by immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) with confirmatory sweat chloride and/or CFTR genetics.

sections.heading: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
items: First-tier marker: TREC (T-cell receptor excision circles) measured on the dried bloodspot - low/absent TRECs indicate poor T-cell output
Aim: detect SCID before infections so infants can be isolated from infection and referred for definitive treatment (haematopoietic stem cell transplant)
Live vaccines (e.g. BCG, rotavirus) must be avoided until SCID is excluded in a screen-positive infant

steps.detail: Raised immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) on the bloodspot (elevated in CF), often followed by CFTR mutation analysis on the same sample (IRT/DNA algorithm).
A positive screen requires a confirmatory SWEAT TEST (raised sweat chloride is the diagnostic standard) +/- genetic testing; fewer than ~10% of screen-positives have CF.

redFlags: SCID screen-positive (low TRECs) - urgent immunology referral, protective isolation, NO live vaccines until excluded
CF screen-positive - timely confirmatory sweat test and specialist referral
A normal screen does not exclude disease in a symptomatic infant - investigate clinically

title: Red reflex test
summary: The red reflex test screens for vision- and life-threatening eye abnormalities (notably congenital cataract and retinoblastoma) by transmitting light through the eye's clear media. The AAP recommends it before nursery discharge and at every routine well-child visit. An abnormal reflex is an ophthalmic emergency.

steps.detail: Darkened room; direct ophthalmoscope set to '0', held close to the examiner's eye, light projected onto both eyes simultaneously from about 18 inches (45 cm).
Look for a bright, symmetrical reddish-orange reflex from each eye; compare both eyes (the Bruckner test compares symmetry of the two reflexes).
Normal = symmetric red reflexes. Abnormal = absent, white (leucocoria), asymmetric, or dark spots - any of these needs urgent ophthalmology referral.

redFlags: White reflex (leucocoria) or absent red reflex - urgent same-day ophthalmology (retinoblastoma is life-threatening; congenital cataract needs early surgery)
Asymmetric reflexes (Bruckner) - refer (anisometropia, strabismus, media opacity)
Any opacity in the visual axis

title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH): Ortolani and Barlow screening
summary: Clinical screening for developmental dysplasia of the hip uses the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres in infants up to ~3 months, plus assessment of abduction and leg-length/skin-fold asymmetry beyond that age. Early detection allows non-surgical treatment (e.g. Pavlik harness).

steps.detail: Infant supine and relaxed; flex the hips to 90 degrees, examine one hip at a time. Place the thumb on the medial proximal thigh and the fingers over the greater trochanter.

Gently ABDUCT the flexed hip while lifting the trochanter - a dislocated femoral head reduces into the acetabulum with a palpable 'clunk' (positive Ortolani). This is the key test for a dislocated hip.
ADDUCT the flexed hip with gentle posterior pressure - a dislocatable hip slips out of the socket (positive Barlow).

sections.heading: Beyond the newborn period / other signs
items: After ~3 months Ortolani/Barlow become unreliable; assess for limited or asymmetric hip abduction, leg-length discrepancy (Galeazzi sign), asymmetric thigh/gluteal skin folds, and a limp/waddling gait when walking
Risk factors (breech, family history, oligohydramnios, female) lower the threshold for ultrasound
Hip ultrasound is the imaging of choice under ~4.5-6 months; X-ray thereafter

redFlags: Positive Ortolani or Barlow - refer to paediatric orthopaedics and arrange hip ultrasound
Limited/asymmetric hip abduction, leg-length difference, or asymmetric skin folds - refer for imaging
Risk factors (breech, positive family history) even with normal exam - arrange screening ultrasound per local protocol

title: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) screening
summary: Examination for testicular descent is part of the newborn and 6-8 week checks. Up to ~90% of undescended testes descend spontaneously by 6 months; those still undescended at 6 months (corrected age) should be referred, as spontaneous descent is then unlikely and orchidopexy preserves fertility and reduces malignancy risk.

sections.heading: Examination and findings
items: Examine in a warm room with warm hands; palpate from the inguinal region toward the scrotum to detect and milk down the testis
Distinguish a retractile testis (can be brought to the scrotum and stays, usually normal) from a true undescended (palpable but not reaching scrotum) or impalpable testis
Re-examine at the 6-8 week check and at the 6-month review

steps.detail: If a testis remains undescended at 6 months (corrected for gestational age), refer to paediatric surgery/urology - spontaneous descent is then unlikely.
Surgical orchidopexy is recommended between about 6 and 18 months; earlier surgery improves testicular growth and fertility potential.
Bilateral non-palpable testes (especially with hypospadias) require urgent assessment to exclude a disorder of sex development / congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

redFlags: Bilateral impalpable testes (with or without hypospadias) - urgent endocrine/surgical assessment (possible DSD / CAH, which can be life-threatening)
Testis undescended at 6 months - refer; do not adopt prolonged watchful waiting
An acutely painful, swollen, 'undescended' or absent testis - consider torsion (emergency)

title: Oral health screening and caries-risk assessment in children
summary: Primary-care oral health screening, caries-risk assessment and fluoride varnish reduce early childhood caries, the most common chronic disease of childhood. The AAP/AAPD/ADA recommend a first dental visit by 1 year of age and dental home establishment.

sections.heading: What to do in primary care
items: Begin oral health risk assessment from around the 6-month visit (AAP oral health risk assessment tool)
Examine for early signs of caries (white-spot lesions, brown spots, cavities), plaque, and gingival health
Assess risk factors: bottle/breast at sleep, frequent sugary drinks/snacks, lack of fluoride, special needs, family caries history
Recommend a first dental visit by age 1 year and establishment of a dental home

steps.detail: Apply fluoride varnish to all children under 5 years (moderate net benefit per USPSTF); higher-risk children benefit most.
Brush twice daily with an age-appropriate amount of fluoride toothpaste, avoid bottle/sippy cup at sleep and frequent sugary intake, and supervise brushing.

redFlags: Visible cavities, brown/black lesions, dental abscess, facial swelling or dental pain - refer to dentist (urgently if abscess/swelling)
Early childhood (nursing/bottle) caries pattern on upper incisors - dental referral and feeding advice
No dental home by ~1 year in a high-risk child

title: Iron-deficiency anaemia screening in young children
summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in young children and can impair neurodevelopment. The AAP recommends universal screening with haemoglobin plus a risk assessment at about 12 months of age (the USPSTF found insufficient evidence for universal screening; selective high-risk screening is also used).

sections.heading: Screening
items: AAP: universal haemoglobin screening at ~12 months of age, combined with an iron-deficiency risk assessment

Risk factors: prematurity/low birthweight, exclusive breastfeeding beyond ~4-6 months without iron supplementation, low intake of iron-rich foods, excessive cow's milk, low socioeconomic status, lead exposure
If anaemic, evaluate with iron studies/ferritin (acute-phase reactant - interpret with CRP) and a dietary history

steps.detail: Treat confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia with oral iron and dietary change; recheck haemoglobin/response after treatment.
Counsel on iron-rich complementary foods from ~6 months, limit cow's milk in toddlers, and consider iron supplementation in preterm/low-birthweight infants.

redFlags: Severe anaemia, poor feeding, or failure to respond to oral iron - investigate further (e.g. coeliac disease, blood loss, haemoglobinopathy)
Microcytic anaemia not responding to iron - reconsider thalassaemia and other causes
Concurrent developmental concern with iron deficiency - treat promptly

title: Blood lead screening in children
summary: Lead exposure harms neurodevelopment with no safe level. The CDC uses a blood lead reference value (BLRV) of 3.5 micrograms/dL (the 97.5th percentile for US children 1-5 years) to identify children with higher-than-typical levels who need follow-up. Targeted testing is commonly done at 12 and 24 months.

sections.heading: Who and when to test
items: CDC/CMS: test Medicaid-enrolled children at 12 and 24 months (or 24-72 months if not previously tested)

Test children with risk factors: older/deteriorating housing, recent renovation, lead-glazed pottery, certain imported cosmetics/remedies/spices, a sibling with elevated lead, or other identified exposure
Capillary screen-positive results should be confirmed with a venous sample

steps.detail: Confirm with venous test; take an environmental exposure history to find and remove the source, give nutrition counselling (adequate iron and calcium reduce absorption), and monitor developmental milestones.
Higher blood lead levels require more intensive case management and, at very high levels, consideration of chelation therapy under specialist guidance.

redFlags: Very high blood lead with encephalopathy signs (vomiting, lethargy, seizures) - medical emergency, urgent specialist/toxicology input
Persistent elevation - identify and remove the ongoing source
Elevated lead with developmental concern - assess and support

title: HEEADSSS adolescent psychosocial screening
summary: HEEADSSS is a structured, developmentally appropriate psychosocial interview for adolescents that moves from less threatening to more sensitive topics to build rapport and identify risk and protective factors. It is used at routine adolescent health contacts to screen for risk-taking and mental-health concerns.

sections.heading: The HEEADSSS domains
items: Home - living situation, relationships, safety at home
Education / Employment - school/work engagement, performance, bullying
Eating - diet, body image, disordered eating
Activities - peers, hobbies, screen/social-media use
Drugs - tobacco, alcohol, other substances (self and peers/family)
Sexuality - relationships, sexual activity, contraception, orientation, abuse
Suicide / depression - mood, self-harm, suicidal ideation (screen explicitly)
Safety - violence, weapons, road/online safety, abuse

steps.detail: Offer time alone with the adolescent and explain confidentiality and its limits (risk of serious harm to self/others) at the outset.

Progress from least to most sensitive topics; identify strengths and protective factors as well as risks, and act on disclosures (e.g. safety planning, referral) - explicitly assess suicide/self-harm.

redFlags: Suicidal ideation, plan, or self-harm - assess risk and arrange urgent mental-health support / safety plan
Disclosure of abuse, exploitation, or violence - safeguarding response
High-risk substance use, unsafe sexual activity, or an unsafe home - intervene and refer
